catalog_quote: Stress in Usen Barok is normally represented by greater intensity and longer duration on vowels. Further instrumental analysis is required to see if pitch also plays a part in stress. Stress is used as a criterion to define the phonological word. Generally speaking, a phonological word contains just one primary stress. The primary stress in Usen Barok almost always falls on the final syllable of a phonological word (with a few exceptions). And the secondary stress in three and four syllable words falls on the first syllable. Illustrative examples are given in Table 2-15. [Table 2-15: monosyllable wan ['wan] 'move'; disyllable löxöön [lɔ.'γɔ:n] 'beach'; trisyllable tinenge [ˌti.ne.'ŋe] 'utterance'; four syllables pösixine [ˌpɔ.si.γi.'ne] 'to smell'] A phonological word with more than four syllables is rare. Example (2-37) gives a phonological word with five syllables in my corpus. ... The primary stress falls on the final syllable of the word, and the secondary stress falls on the second syllable (the last syllable of bunbun 'all'). (2-37) bunbunnarama [bun.ˌbun.na.ra.'ma] 'the whole family' ... [ch. 1, p. 15] The primary stress of a phonological word normally falls on the ultimate syllable. This is different from many Oceanic languages, in which stress generally falls on the penultimate syllable of a word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the phonological word (word-final, fixed); suffixes/enclitics that end the word (applicative -in, stative =sik) carry the primary stress, i.e. stress stays word-final after affixation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of three- and four-syllable words (e.g. [ˌti.ne.'ŋe], [ˌpɔ.si.γi.'ne]); in the five-syllable compound bunbunnarama [bun.ˌbun.na.ra.'ma] secondary stress is on the second syllable (last syllable of the first member).
new_statements.exceptions: 'with a few exceptions' (not enumerated); one stress-based minimal pair: ine [i.'ne] 3SG independent pronoun vs ['i.ne] personal noun-phrase marker (initial stress). Author notes final stress is unlike the penultimate stress common in Oceanic languages.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (stress is the author's criterion for phonological wordhood; one primary stress per phonological word); enclitic =sik and suffix -in are inside the domain and take the final stress. Impressionistic (no instrumental study; author says pitch correlates need instrumental analysis). Describes the Usen dialect only.
new_statements.identity_note: Du 2010 describes the Usen dialect of Barok (east coast: Kolonoboi, Belik, Kanapit etc.); the other dialect, Nabo (= 'Central' Barok in SIL's listing), is not described. Glottolog baro1253 has no dialect-level sub-codes, so the statement is filed under baro1253 with the Usen restriction noted.
